topics.verify: Source range. PDF 696–700 (notebook 179–181), the source's lub-oil analysis block. Source errors corrected. (1) RDE, not 'ROE' (P29-C007): the arc/spark spectrometer is the Rotating Disc Electrode atomic emission spectrometer (RDE-AES, ASTM D6595). (2) Elemental technique (P29-C005): atomic emission spectroscopy is the usual principle, but CIMAC also lists atomic absorption and X-ray fluorescence; AES is not the only method. (3) FTIR (P29-C013): the source says the absorbed infrared light is taken up 'by the particles'. Infrared is absorbed by molecules — chemical bonds at characteristic wavenumbers — so FTIR measures oxidation products, water, glycol, fuel and soot loading; it does not measure particles. (4) Particle counting (P29-C015): the source presents particle counts as a proactive wear warning for oil generally. CIMAC states that the optical ISO 4406/NAS methods were developed for hydraulic oils, are not very suitable for dark, sooty used engine oils (dilution up to 1:10, large scatter) and are not routine for engine oils; the proactive value applies mainly to hydraulic, gear and turbine oils. (5) Low BN (P29-C021): the source reads low BN as 'blow-by'. Low BN means the alkaline reserve has been consumed by sulphuric acid from fuel sulphur (carried to the crankcase oil by blow-by in trunk-piston engines); causes include high-sulphur fuel, low oil consumption or top-up, and the wrong grade. Removed. The source's line that BN and AN tests are 'relatively expensive with poor results' (P29-C023) is not taught: they are routine, standard titrations central to CIMAC interpretation. Added from the held CIMAC texts (Recommendation No. 30, 2011, and the WG8 guideline, February 2023): viscosity, water, flash point, insolubles, the PQ index, sampling practice and the two-stroke system-oil and scrape-down interpretation tables. Standards are cited by number and name only; edition years are deliberately omitted.
topics.definition: Used-oil analysis is the laboratory (or shipboard) testing of a sample of in-service lubricating oil to answer two questions at once: is the oil still fit for use, and — to a certain extent — what condition is the machinery it lubricates in. The tests fall into three families: fluid properties (viscosity, base number, acid number, oxidation), contamination (water, fuel, soot and insolubles, glycol, sea-water and fuel elements) and wear debris (wear metals and ferrous particles). The core methods are elemental spectrometric analysis (ICP or RDE atomic emission, reported in ppm), FTIR (infrared absorption by molecules), particle counting (ISO cleanliness code) and the BN/AN titrations. A single result rarely diagnoses anything: the value of oil analysis lies in the trend from the same sampling point, laboratory and method.
why: Simon asks what the report means, not what the laboratory does. The Chief Engineer must read a spectrometric, FTIR and BN result together and say what is happening in the engine — and what he will do next.

The limitations are where candidates fail. ICP does not see particles larger than about 5–7 µm, so iron can look steady while a bearing or liner is failing; a particle count on dark engine oil is unreliable; BN from two different titration methods cannot be compared.

System oil on a two-stroke is a shared fluid. It lubricates bearings, cools pistons and, on an ME engine, is the hydraulic medium for the HPS and HCUs — a stuffing-box leak, a cooler leak or a leaking fuel pump all show first in the oil report.
Oil analysis is condition-based maintenance evidence. It justifies opening up, or not opening up, a unit and supports the maintenance decision under the company's planned maintenance system.

sections.head: 🧪 Why Analyse Used Oil — Two Purposes, Three Families of Test

body.p: The source opens with the two purposes of analysis — the condition of the oil and the working condition of the machinery from which the sample was taken — and the three categories of test. CIMAC adds the honest qualifier: analysis shows oil condition and suitability for further use reliably, and machinery condition only to a certain extent, and only when the sample is representative.

head: Family
What it tells you
Typical tests
rows: Is the oil itself still fit — viscosity, alkaline reserve, ageing?
Viscosity (kV at 40 °C and/or 100 °C), BN, AN, FTIR oxidation / nitration / sulphation
What has got into the oil, and from where?

Water (Karl Fischer or infrared), flash point (fuel dilution), insolubles, soot, glycol; contaminant elements Na, K, B, Mg, Cl (water / coolant / sea water), V and Ni (residual fuel), Si (dust, cat fines — but also anti-foam additive)
Which components are wearing, and how fast?
Wear elements Fe, Cr, Cu, Pb, Sn, Al, Mo, Sb by spectrometry; PQ index and ferrography for larger ferrous particles

body.p: Sampling decides everything. CIMAC's key points: sample with the machine running at normal temperature; from the main supply line at the engine inlet, in full flow (a side or top tapping on a horizontal pipe, not the bottom); always from the same point; flush about 0.5–1.0 litre through the valve first; fill a clean, dedicated bottle (about 250 ml, or about 100 ml for two-stroke scavenge drain oil) to about 90%; label it fully (engine, oil, sampling point, date, running hours) and dispatch it promptly. Sample monthly until a trend is established and then at intervals set by the OEM or oil supplier, normally not more than three months apart — and always at intervals shorter than the expected time to failure of the condition being watched.

sections.head: ⚛️ Elemental (Spectrometric) Analysis — ICP and RDE

body.p: Principle. In atomic emission spectroscopy the oil sample is exposed to a high-energy source — an electric arc/spark or a plasma. The atoms are excited and, as they relax, emit light at wavelengths characteristic of each element. The intensity at each element's wavelength, calibrated against oil-soluble metal standards, gives its concentration, reported in ppm (mg/kg). This is the most fundamental routine test, which is why the source also calls it wear-metal analysis — but it measures additive elements and contaminants as well as wear metals. CIMAC lists three spectroscopic routes: atomic emission (the usual one), atomic absorption and X-ray fluorescence.

head: ICP-AES (inductively coupled plasma)
RDE-AES (rotating disc electrode)
rows: Argon plasma; sample nebulised into it
Arc/spark between a disc electrode rotating through the oil and a counter-electrode
The method mostly used by shore laboratories (CIMAC)
Particles larger than about 5–7 µm are not fully vaporised and are not detected
Also particle-size-limited; large wear particles are under-read

body.p: What the elements point to (CIMAC Rec. 30): additive elements Ca, Mg, P, Zn (and Si) identify the oil and reveal mixing with another grade; wear elements Al, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mo, Pb, Sb, Sn indicate wear of bearings, rings, liners and other components; contaminants K, Mg, B, Cl and Na come from water, condensate, sea water or coolant, V and Ni from residual fuel, and Si from dust or sand as well as from anti-foam additive.

The limitation that matters. Because ICP misses particles above about 5–7 µm, wear-metal readings can flatten — or even fall — while a severe wear process accelerates and produces larger debris. CIMAC's remedy is non-routine analysis: the PQ index (a magnetometric measure of total ferrous debris, independent of particle size and most sensitive above about 20 µm), ferrography (ferrous particles aligned by size for expert examination of the wear mechanism — cutting, fatigue, adhesion), or ashing / XRF to capture all the material. CIMAC also warns that results depend on apparatus and preparation, so trends must use the same laboratory, apparatus and method, and that low values (below 5 ppm) should be read with caution.

sections.head: 🌈 FTIR — Infrared Absorption by Molecules

body.p: Principle. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy is a purely instrument-based test. Every chemical bond absorbs infrared energy at its own characteristic frequencies (the source's 'resonance frequencies'), expressed as wavenumbers in cm−1. A thin film of the used oil is placed in the infrared cell; the transmitted spectrum is compared with the incident beam and with a new-oil reference of the same product, and the absorbance at each characteristic wavenumber measures how much of that molecular species is present. Infrared is absorbed by molecules, not by particles — FTIR does not count or size particles.

head: Parameter
Absorption region (CIMAC Rec. 30)
What a rise means
rows: Oil ageing by oxygen and temperature; viscosity and AN usually rise with it
Reaction with NOx in blow-by — measured mainly on gas-engine and high-speed engine oils
Reaction with sulphur oxides; rises as BN falls
Poor combustion, burnt lube oil, worn injectors, inadequate oil treatment
Trend indicators — quantify water by Karl Fischer titration

body.p: ASTM E2412 describes FTIR as a trend-analysis practice: additive depletion, contaminants (water, soot, glycol, fuels, incorrect oil) and base-stock degradation (oxidation, nitration, sulphation). CIMAC stresses that a fresh-oil baseline is needed and that only results from the same laboratory and method should be compared.

sections.head: 🔬 Particle Counting and the ISO Cleanliness Code

body.p: What it measures. Particle counting gives the number and size distribution of solid particles in the oil — a direct measure of cleanliness. Automatic optical counters use light obscuration or scattering (laser); the microscope method (ISO 4407) is older but still a current standard and a referee method for dark or heavily contaminated fluids, so 'old method' should not be read as 'obsolete'. Pore-blockage counters are a further type used for dark oils.

body.ascii:
ISO 4406 cleanliness code (automatic counter calibrated to ISO 11171)
   three scale numbers  =  particles per mL  ≥ 4 µm(c) / ≥ 6 µm(c) / ≥ 14 µm(c)
   e.g. 18/16/13  (illustrative)      each step up the scale ≈ DOUBLES the count
   microscope count (ISO 4407) is reported as a two-number code at ≥ 5 µm and ≥ 15 µm
   alternative scales: NAS 1638, SAE AS4059

body.p: Where it works and where it does not. For hydraulic, gear and turbine oils particle counting is the proactive measure: a rising code warns of filter or purifier failure, ingress and early wear before damage. For used engine oils CIMAC is explicit: the ISO 4406/NAS optical methods were developed for hydraulic oils, are not very suitable for dark, sooty engine oils that must be diluted as much as 1:10, give significant scatter, and are therefore not routine. Wear in engine oils is tracked mainly by spectrometry, the PQ index and ferrography. The link to the engine room: on an ME engine the system oil is also the hydraulic oil for the hydraulic power supply and cylinder units, and the CIMAC two-stroke table lists a rising particle count among the risks to hydraulic system components (Topic 3).

sections.head: ⚖️ Base Number vs Acid Number

body.p: Definitions. Acid number (AN, formerly TAN) is the amount of acidic material in the oil; base number (BN, formerly TBN) is its alkaline reserve — the capacity left to neutralise acids from combustion. Both are expressed in mg KOH/g and found by potentiometric titration: AN by titration with potassium hydroxide (ASTM D664); BN by titration with an acid — perchloric acid (ASTM D2896, the usual method for new and marine engine oils, giving the higher value) or hydrochloric acid (ASTM D4739, often used for used oils). The two BN methods are not interchangeable, so a trend must stay on one method.

head: Base Number (BN)
Acid Number (AN)
rows: Alkaline reserve left to neutralise acids
Acidic content formed or picked up
Crankcase / trunk-piston engine oils; two-stroke system oil; cylinder scrape-down oil (residual BN with iron, for cylinder condition)
Turbine, hydraulic, gear and compressor oils; also relevant for low-BN engine oils and gas-engine oils (CIMAC)
Falling BN: alkaline reserve consumed by sulphuric acid from fuel sulphur. Rising BN in two-stroke system oil: cylinder oil leaking in past the piston-rod stuffing box (or a high-BN oil added)
Rising AN: oxidation, or contamination with acidic products; biofuel operation can also raise it. High-AN oil can be corrosive
Low BN: corrosive wear of liners, rings and bearings

body.p: Low BN, correctly explained. Sulphur in the fuel burns to SO2 with a little SO3; with the water formed by combustion these condense as sulphuric acid, which the oil's alkaline additives neutralise. In a trunk-piston engine the acidic combustion products reach the crankcase oil with the blow-by gas. BN depletion is therefore driven by fuel sulphur, by oil consumption (fresh top-up restores alkalinity) and by operating conditions — a low BN is not by itself a measure of blow-by, and a wrong oil grade is always a possibility.

Method, not cost, is the limitation. BN and AN are routine, inexpensive titrations, and shipboard BN kits are standard for scrape-down and system-oil checks. The real caution is that the value depends on the test method — trend results from one laboratory and one method only.

sections.head: 🛢️ The Rest of a Routine Report — Viscosity, Water, Flash Point, Insolubles

body.p: The source's handwritten notes stop at BN and AN, but a routine CIMAC report always carries these four characteristics, and an oral answer on 'what does the report show' is incomplete without them.

head: Characteristic
How measured
Reading it
rows: Kinematic viscosity by capillary flow time, at 40 °C and/or 100 °C (mm²/s, cSt)

Increase: oxidation, residual-fuel contamination (asphaltenes), soot and insolubles, water emulsion, top-up with a heavier oil. Decrease — potentially more harmful, because film thickness falls: dilution by light (distillate) fuel or top-up with a thinner oil. On a two-stroke, system oil may also be thickened by cylinder oil from the stuffing box.
Karl Fischer titration or infrared (preferred to distillation)

Cooler or jacket leakage, condensation, a badly set separator. Sea water (Na with Mg) is corrosive; emulsions reduce load-carrying capacity. CIMAC's four-stroke guidance treats water above 0.2% v/v as the point to check the centrifuge and find the source.
Open-cup or closed-cup method (closed cup reads lower)

A drop indicates distillate fuel dilution; residual fuel may show little change. CIMAC's four-stroke guidance: check for fuel leakage when the flash point drops by 30 °C or more; gas chromatography measures fuel dilution more precisely. Flash point is not a measure of crankcase-explosion risk.
Solid material separated by solvent (pentane, heptane or toluene) and filtration or centrifuging
A composite of contamination and degradation, not a particle count; different methods give different values. Rises with poor combustion, fuel contamination, purifier or filter problems.

sections.head: 📈 Reading the Report — Trend, Limits and Limitations

ul: One analysis is not a diagnosis. CIMAC: a full and proper diagnosis cannot be achieved from the results of just one analysis. Plot each parameter against time or running hours and look for a change of trend — 'it is the trend that is most important'.

Limits are guidance. 'Caution' and 'action/urgent' limits come from the OEM and the oil supplier (OEM limits first, at least during warranty) and must be refined system by system as data builds up. Reliance on arbitrary limits gives false security.
Fast failures escape it. Oil analysis is less effective where the failure develops quickly — liner scuffing or a bearing fracture — because the sampling interval is longer than the time to failure.
Same point, same laboratory, same method. Spectrometry, insolubles, BN and FTIR are all method-dependent; a change of laboratory resets the baseline.
Context. The analyst needs engine running hours, oil top-up, fuel changes and any incident — the engine staff's information is part of the diagnosis.

body.p: Oil analysis is one of the condition-monitoring tools that make predictive maintenance possible — see the preventive-versus-predictive comparison in Simon Notes Part 4 · Note 35; Part 16 links oil analysis and vibration data to maintenance decisions in Part 16 · Topic 4.

ce_tip.text: Simon asks 'What is lube oil analysis and what do you do with the report?' Answer in four moves. One: two purposes and three families — oil condition and machinery condition; fluid properties, contamination, wear debris. Two: the methods with their principle — spectrometry (atomic emission, ICP or RDE, ppm), FTIR (infrared absorbed by molecules: oxidation, nitration, sulphation, soot, water), particle count (ISO 4406, for clean oils), BN and AN titrations. Three: the limitation — ICP is blind above about 5–7 µm, so a flat iron trend does not prove a healthy engine; ask for PQ or ferrography. Four: action from the trend — e.g. system-oil BN and viscosity rising together means stuffing-box leakage, so check the drains and the rings. Three answers lose marks: 'ROE', 'FTIR detects particles', and 'BN and AN tests are expensive and useless'.

qa: Q1. What is used lube-oil analysis, and what are its main categories?

Used-oil analysis is the testing of a representative sample of in-service oil to assess the condition of the oil and, to a certain extent, the condition of the machinery it lubricates. The tests fall into three families. Fluid properties tell me whether the oil is still fit: viscosity, base number, acid number and the FTIR degradation measures — oxidation, nitration and sulphation. Contamination tells me what has entered the oil: water, fuel shown by a falling flash point or viscosity, soot and insolubles, glycol, and contaminant elements such as sodium and magnesium from sea water or vanadium and nickel from residual fuel. Wear debris tells me which components are wearing: wear metals by spectrometry, supported by the PQ index or ferrography for larger ferrous particles. The sample must come from the same full-flow point at the engine inlet, with the engine running at temperature and the valve flushed, and the result is read as a trend, never as a single value.
Q2. Explain elemental spectrometric analysis and its main limitation.

Elemental analysis measures the concentration of metals in the oil in ppm, that is milligrams per kilogram. It is normally done by atomic emission spectroscopy: the sample is exposed to a high-energy source, an argon plasma in ICP or an arc between a rotating disc electrode and a counter electrode in RDE. The excited atoms emit light at wavelengths characteristic of each element, and the intensity at each wavelength, calibrated against standards, gives the concentration. Atomic absorption and X-ray fluorescence are also used. The results cover additive elements such as calcium and zinc, wear metals such as iron, chromium, copper, lead and tin, and contaminants such as sodium, vanadium and silicon. The key limitation is particle size: ICP does not detect particles larger than about 5 to 7 microns, so in severe wear the iron reading can stay flat while large debris is being produced. I would then ask for the PQ index, ferrography or an ashed sample. Results also depend on the laboratory and method, and values below about 5 ppm need caution.
Q3. How does FTIR work, and what does it detect?

FTIR is infrared spectroscopy of the oil film. Different chemical bonds absorb infrared at characteristic wavenumbers. The instrument passes infrared through a thin layer of the used oil, compares the transmitted spectrum with the incident beam and with a new-oil reference, and the absorbance at each wavenumber gives the amount of that molecular species. It therefore measures molecules, not particles. CIMAC uses about 1710 inverse centimetres for oxidation, 1620 for nitration and 1150 for sulphation; FTIR also shows soot, water, glycol and fuel as trend indicators, with Karl Fischer titration used to quantify water. It is a trend tool against a fresh-oil baseline, standardised as a condition-monitoring practice in ASTM E2412.
Q4. Distinguish base number and acid number. What does a low BN in a trunk-piston engine oil indicate?

Both are in milligrams of KOH per gram and found by potentiometric titration. Acid number measures the acidic content of the oil and is the main degradation test for turbine, hydraulic, gear and compressor oils, and is also relevant for low-BN and gas-engine oils; it rises mainly with oxidation. Base number measures the alkaline reserve left to neutralise acids and is the key test for engine oils. BN by perchloric acid and by hydrochloric acid are different methods and must not be mixed in a trend. Low BN in a trunk-piston engine means the alkaline reserve has been used up by sulphuric acid formed from fuel sulphur, which reaches the crankcase with the blow-by gas. Causes are high-sulphur fuel, low oil consumption so too little fresh oil is added, or the wrong grade. The risk is corrosive wear of liners, rings and bearings. Low BN is not in itself a measure of blow-by.
Q5. Your two-stroke main engine system-oil report shows BN and viscosity both rising over three samples. What is happening and what do you do?

Rising BN together with rising viscosity in two-stroke system oil is the classic signature of cylinder oil, which has a much higher BN, leaking down into the crankcase past the piston-rod stuffing boxes; a top-up with a different, higher-BN oil is the other possibility, so I first check the top-up record. Then I check the stuffing-box drain quantities cylinder by cylinder, compare them with the maker's guidance and look for the unit with abnormal leakage, plan inspection and overhaul of the stuffing-box rings, and review cylinder-oil feed rate and scavenge-space condition. Meanwhile I watch insolubles and viscosity, run the purifier correctly, and if the oil drifts towards the supplier's action limit I discuss partial renewal. I ask the laboratory for a follow-up sample after the repair to confirm the trend has turned.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — The Iron Reading That Stayed Flat
blocks: A four-stroke auxiliary engine's monthly reports show iron steady at a familiar level for four samples. The engine is running hotter on one main bearing temperature, and the oil filter differential pressure rises faster than usual. The third engineer's summary reads 'oil analysis normal'.
What the Chief Engineer reads into it

The method. The shore laboratory uses ICP, which does not detect particles larger than about 5–7 µm. A developing bearing or journal failure produces larger debris, so the spectrometric iron can stay flat — or even fall — while the real wear rate rises. CIMAC describes exactly this pattern against a rising PQ index. The other evidence. A rising bearing temperature and a filter loading faster than normal are independent signals that larger particles are being generated. What to ask for. A PQ index and ferrography on the next sample, plus inspection of the filter element and its debris, and a check of the copper, lead and tin trends for bearing-metal involvement.

The Chief Engineer does not wait for the next routine sample: the evidence justifies opening the suspect bearing under the planned maintenance system. The general lesson for the oral is that oil analysis is one instrument among several. A 'normal' spectrometric result does not over-rule temperatures, filter behaviour or noise, and the limitation of each method must be known before the result is trusted.

topics.verify: Source range. PDF 701–706 (notebook 182–184), the source's short-notes block. Source errors corrected. (1) Instrument (P29-C024): 'MEPC 312(74)' is resolution MEPC.312(74), adopted 17 May 2019, Guidelines for the use of electronic record books under MARPOL. It covers MARPOL record books only; deck, engine and official logbooks in electronic form are a flag-State matter, so the heading 'Electronic Logbook' is broader than the instrument. (2) Seven, not six, records (P29-C025): the source omits the recording of the Tier and on/off status of marine diesel engines (Annex VI reg. 13.5.3). (3) Updating (P29-C031): the guideline does not merely ask for periodic review — the system must incorporate MARPOL amendments before they enter into force, without losing existing records. (4) The source's own OWS example for 'complete before saving' (P29-C026) is replaced by IMO's example, an Annex V discharge that cannot be saved without the position. (5) MASS benefits (P29-C040): 'enhanced safety as no human error' is overstated — remote operators and software still err, and MASS adds connectivity, cyber and sensor risks. (6) Who develops the non-mandatory MASS Code (P29-C041): it is an MSC instrument; the MSC-LEG-FAL Joint Working Group handles only the cross-cutting issues. (7) JWG 3 (P29-C042) was a separate meeting on 8–10 May 2024, before MSC 108, not held 'in' MSC 108. The mandatory code is a target only (P29-C047). (9) Maritime 'Safety' Window (P29-C049) is a slip for Maritime Single Window, and the obligation falls on Contracting Governments to the FAL Convention, not on 'all IMO Member States'. (10) BBNJ is not a plastics treaty (P29-C057). (11) 'Navigating the Future: Safety First' (P29-C060) was IMO's World Maritime Day theme for 2024, not India's National Maritime Day theme. Closed on primary text by the coordinator (closure log 8 Oct 2026). The 2022 FAL amendments are resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, in force 1 January 2024; the Indian instrument is DG Shipping (now DGMA) Merchant Shipping Notice No. 03 of 2024 (9 February 2024), 'Use of Electronic Record Books Under MARPOL'.
topics.definition: Electronic record books are approved software systems that replace the paper MARPOL record books, under IMO's Guidelines for the use of electronic record books under MARPOL (resolution MEPC.312(74)) and the MARPOL amendments that permit them. Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are ships that, to a varying degree, can operate independently of human interaction; IMO describes four degrees of autonomy, and the non-mandatory MASS Code adopted at MSC 111 in May 2026 is the first goal-based safety framework for them, with a mandatory code only a future target. The Maritime Single Window (MSW) is the single electronic portal through which a port State's authorities receive and exchange the information required for a ship's arrival, stay and departure — mandatory for FAL Contracting Governments since 1 January 2024, and implemented in India as a module of SagarSetu (NLP-Marine). Annual maritime days and their themes are dated current-affairs facts and are kept in the calendar box below.
why: Nair asks for the regulation behind the gadget. 'Can the Oil Record Book be electronic?' is answered with MEPC.312(74), the seven record books it covers, the approval and the Declaration on board — not with a vendor's feature list.

The Chief Engineer signs the engine-room record books. An electronic system shifts the risks from ink and missing pages to log-ins, audit trails, back-ups and certified printouts that a PSC officer may demand.

MASS is a current-affairs favourite with a trap. The non-mandatory MASS Code now exists; the mandatory code does not. Candidates who call the current code mandatory, or the future code adopted, lose the examiner.
MSW changes the pre-arrival workload. Port-clearance data now flows electronically through one window; in India that window sits inside SagarSetu, the National Logistics Portal (Marine).

sections.head: 💻 Electronic Record Books — What MEPC.312(74) Covers

body.p: The source heads this note 'Electronic Logbook'. The IMO instrument is narrower: resolution MEPC.312(74), adopted on 17 May 2019, gives Guidelines for the use of electronic record books under MARPOL, supporting the MARPOL amendments (in force 1 October 2020) that allow the record books to be kept electronically in a method approved by the Administration. Paragraph 2.1 lists seven records:

head: Record book (MEPC.312(74) para 2.1)
MARPOL basis
rows: Oil Record Book, Parts I and II
Garbage Record Book, Parts I and II
Recording of the Tier and on/off status of marine diesel engines (omitted in the source)

body.p: Not covered. The deck log, engine-room log and official logbook are not MARPOL record books. Whether they may be electronic is decided by the flag State. Ballast-water record keeping sits under the BWM Convention, not MEPC.312(74).

sections.head: 🤖 MASS — Definition and the Four Degrees of Autonomy

body.p: IMO uses MASS for 'a ship which, to a varying degree, can operate independent of human interaction'. For its regulatory scoping exercise (MSC.1/Circ.1638, 3 June 2021) IMO described four degrees of autonomy. They were set for the purpose of that exercise, they are not hierarchical, and a ship may operate at more than one degree during a single voyage.

head: Degree
Description
Seafarers on board?
rows: Ship with automated processes and decision support — some operations automated and at times unsupervised, but seafarers ready to take control
Remotely controlled ship with seafarers on board — controlled from another location
Remotely controlled ship without seafarers on board
Fully autonomous ship — the operating system makes decisions and determines actions by itself

body.p: Benefits and risks, balanced. Claimed benefits are lower crewing cost, a possible reduction in accidents caused by on-board human error and fatigue, efficiency gains from optimised route and speed, and operational flexibility. They are offset by new risks: loss of connectivity, cyber attack, sensor reliability and remote-operator error. Human error is moved ashore, not removed — which is why the non-mandatory MASS Code is built on goal-based safety requirements rather than an assumption of 'no human error'.

sections.head: 📜 The MASS Code — Status as of 8 October 2026

ul: Who develops it. The non-mandatory MASS Code is a Maritime Safety Committee instrument, developed through the MSC's MASS working and correspondence groups. A joint MSC-LEG-FAL Working Group (JWG) handles the issues that cut across the three committees' instruments — the role of the master, the remote operator and responsibility. JWG 3 met separately on 8–10 May 2024; its outcome went to MSC 108 and LEG 112.
Road map. MSC 109 (2–6 December 2024) agreed a revised road map.

Adopted. MSC 111 (13–22 May 2026) adopted the non-mandatory International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, which takes effect from 1 July 2026. It applies to cargo ships under SOLAS chapter I; Governments are invited to apply it, as far as practicable, to MASS below 500 GT. Being non-mandatory, it 'takes effect' rather than 'enters into force'.

sections.head: 🌐 Maritime Single Window — FAL Convention and India's SagarSetu

body.p: The source writes 'Maritime Safety Window' once; the instrument is the Maritime Single Window. The FAL Convention moved to digital clearance in two steps: electronic exchange of information became mandatory on 8 April 2019, and the 2022 FAL amendments — resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022 — made a single window mandatory from 1 January 2024. The obligation falls on the public authorities of Contracting Governments to the FAL Convention: they must establish, maintain and use a single window for the electronic exchange of the information required on the arrival, stay and departure of ships, persons and cargo, so that data is submitted once and routed to customs, immigration, health and port authorities. IMO's purpose is faster clearance and greater efficiency of shipping.

India. On 1 February 2024 the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways launched the MSW module, together with the MMD module, in SagarSetu (NLP-Marine), the National Logistics Portal (Marine) whose mobile app was launched in 2023. The MSW module enables electronic submission, processing and exchange of maritime information and documents between government agencies, port authorities, shipping agents and other trade stakeholders, along FAL Convention lines. Sagar Setu is the platform; the MSW is one module within it.
The general MSW definition and India's earlier single-window work are in Simon Notes Part 7 · Note 5; this topic adds the FAL obligation holder and SagarSetu.

ce_tip.text: Nair asks 'Can your Oil Record Book be electronic?' Say yes — under MARPOL as amended in force 1 October 2020, in a method approved by the Administration, following MEPC.312(74). Name the seven records (don't forget the Tier and on/off status record), then the integrity features: unique log-ins, e-signatures, the audit trail with the original and amended values both visible, the master's verified status, the true-copy printout and the Declaration on board. If he moves to MASS, give the four degrees from MSC.1/Circ.1638 and say they are non-hierarchical; then the status in one breath: 'The non-mandatory MASS Code was adopted at MSC 111 and took effect on 1 July 2026; a mandatory code is only targeted — adoption by 2030, entry into force 2032.' Never call today's code mandatory, and never say MSW is 'Maritime Safety Window'.

qa: Q1. Which MARPOL record books may be kept electronically, and under what instrument?

MARPOL, as amended with effect from 1 October 2020, allows record books to be kept electronically in a method approved by the Administration, and IMO's guidelines for doing so are resolution MEPC.312(74), adopted 17 May 2019. Paragraph 2.1 lists seven records: the Oil Record Book Parts I and II, the Cargo Record Book, the Garbage Record Book Parts I and II, the Ozone-depleting Substances Record Book, the recording of the Tier and on/off status of marine diesel engines, the Record of Fuel Oil Changeover, and the Record Book of Engine Parameters under the NOx Technical Code. The guidelines do not cover the deck, engine or official logbooks; whether those may be electronic is a flag-State decision. On board, the ship carries a Declaration issued by or for the flag State confirming that the electronic record book meets the guidelines.
Q2. What features must an approved electronic record book have to make it trustworthy?

It must allow an entry to be saved for verification only when complete — IMO's example is an Annex V discharge that cannot be saved without the ship's position. Data should come in automatically wherever possible, with manual input on sensor failure logged as a change of data source, and the system must protect automatic data and record any attempt at manipulation. Each user needs a unique log-in and password under role-based access control, and entries carry the user's electronic signature, with an additional authentication factor for the master's verification. Every change keeps the original visible with date, time and signature, and an amended verified entry goes back to pending. Records must be kept for the MARPOL period, printable as true copies for the master to certify, backed up, and updated for MARPOL amendments before they enter into force. Receipts such as a sludge barge receipt can be attached.
Q3. Explain the four degrees of autonomy for MASS.

IMO's regulatory scoping exercise, reported in MSC.1/Circ.1638 of June 2021, described four degrees. Degree one is a ship with automated processes and decision support: seafarers are on board to operate and control the systems, some operations may be automated and at times unsupervised, but the crew is ready to take control. Degree two is a remotely controlled ship with seafarers on board who can take over. Degree three is a remotely controlled ship without seafarers on board. Degree four is a fully autonomous ship whose operating system makes decisions and determines actions by itself. The degrees were defined for the scoping exercise, they are not hierarchical, and a ship may operate at different degrees during one voyage, so they should not be presented as a mandatory classification.
Q4. What is the current status of the MASS Code?

The MASS Code is a Maritime Safety Committee instrument. A joint MSC-LEG-FAL working group deals only with the cross-cutting legal and facilitation issues such as the role of the master and the remote operator. MSC 109 in December 2024 agreed a revised road map, and MSC 111, held 13 to 22 May 2026, adopted the non-mandatory International Code of Safety for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships, which took effect on 1 July 2026 for cargo ships under SOLAS chapter I; Governments are invited to apply it as far as practicable to MASS below 500 GT. Next, MSC 112 in December 2026 is to develop the framework for an experience-building phase. Development of a mandatory code is to begin in 2028, with a new SOLAS chapter, and the mandatory code is expected to be adopted by 1 July 2030 and to enter into force on 1 January 2032. Those last dates are targets: no mandatory MASS Code exists today.
Q5. What is the Maritime Single Window, and how has India implemented it?

The Maritime Single Window is the single electronic portal through which a ship or its agent submits the information required for arrival, stay and departure of ship, persons and cargo once, with the data routed to customs, immigration, health and port authorities. Under the FAL Convention, electronic exchange of information became mandatory in April 2019, and the 2022 FAL amendments, resolution FAL.14(46), made the single window mandatory from 1 January 2024 for the public authorities of Contracting Governments. In India, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways launched the MSW module, with the MMD module, on 1 February 2024 inside SagarSetu, the National Logistics Portal (Marine). It allows electronic submission, processing and exchange of maritime information and documents between government agencies, port authorities, agents and trade stakeholders.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — Switching the Oil Record Book to Electronic
blocks: The company announces that from the next port the ship will use an electronic record-book system for the Oil Record Book Part I, the Garbage Record Book and the fuel changeover record. The superintendent asks the Chief Engineer to 'stop the paper books once the software is installed'.
What the Chief Engineer checks first

Approval and Declaration. Is the system approved by or for the flag State, and is the Declaration on board? Without it the paper books remain the legal record. For an Indian-flag ship, the reference is DG Shipping (now DGMA) Merchant Shipping Notice No. 03 of 2024. Scope. The system covers MARPOL record books only; the engine-room log stays as the flag State requires. Users. Every officer has a personal log-in; nobody shares a password; the master's verification uses the extra authentication factor. Integrity. Test an amendment: the original and the corrected value must both remain visible with time and signature, and the entry must return to 'pending'. Evidence. Barge and reception-facility receipts are scanned and attached, and the originals retained. Continuity. Back-up arrangements and a procedure for producing a certified true copy if a PSC officer asks, or if the system fails.

The electronic book changes the form of the record, not the Chief Engineer's responsibility for its truth. Changeover is controlled like any other change under the SMS: a dated cut-over entry, the closed paper books retained for the MARPOL period, and crew trained before the first entry.

topics.verify: Source range. PDF 707–721: ME engines (707–711), latest engine developments (712–720) and turbocharger types (721). OEM name. MAN Energy Solutions was renamed Everllence on 4 June 2025; MAN B&W model names are kept. Source errors corrected — ME platform. (1) Not common rail (P29-C063): each cylinder has its own hydraulically driven fuel booster on its HCU, fed by a common ~300 bar hydraulic-oil supply from the HPS; a fuel common rail is the WinGD RT-flex/X principle. (2) No camshaft (P29-C062) is true of ME-C only; the small-bore ME-B keeps a camshaft for the exhaust valves. (3) HPS and tacho are separate units, not parts of the HCU (P29-C066). (4) MPC is the Multi-Purpose Controller, not a 'card'; loaded with CCU software it is the CCU (P29-C072, P29-C079). (5) FIVA = Fuel Injection and exhaust Valve Activation (P29-C078); ELVA = Electronic exhaust Valve Actuation (P29-C077). Gas engines. (6) Ammonia is injected as a liquid in the ME-LGI family, not burnt as a 'gas' (P29-C085); efficiency is not the main driver (P29-C086); only LNG Otto engines are Tier III in gas mode without after-treatment (P29-C087); the IMO GHG Strategy is MEPC.377(80), not Annex VI, and the fuel-intensity rules are draft (P29-C088). (7) ME-GA pressure (P29-C095): the source's '3–4 bar' is replaced by the OEM figure — engine inlet pressure 'in the range of 5.5–12 barg, depending on engine load and rating' (Everllence project guide 7.00, ME-GA); gas is admitted through SGAVs located in the cylinder liner, not injected. (8) Knock and pre-ignition are different events (P29-C097). (9) ME-GA Tier III (P29-C101, P29-C120, coordinator-reconciled): the ME-GA design specifies EGR as standard (Everllence project guide, 2025), which ensures Tier III in dual-fuel and fuel-oil-only modes; Tier III is not guaranteed in SDF mode. (10) ME-GI is Tier II as built and reaches Tier III with EGR or SCR — not simply 'non-compliant' (P29-C109). NOx. topics.definition: An ME engine (MAN B&W, now Everllence) is a two-stroke crosshead engine in which fuel injection, exhaust-valve actuation and starting air are controlled electronically instead of by a camshaft. Hydraulic oil at about 300 bar from a Hydraulic Power Supply drives, cylinder by cylinder, a fuel-oil pressure booster and an exhaust-valve actuator on each Hydraulic Cylinder Unit; a proportional valve (ELFI and ELVA, or the combined FIVA) commanded by the Cylinder Control Unit sets timing, quantity and rate. The same platform carries the dual-fuel engines: the ME-GI injects gas at high pressure (up to about 300 bar) into the flame of a pilot-oil injection and burns it on the Diesel principle; the ME-GA admits gas at low pressure into the cylinder during compression and ignites the premixed charge with pilot oil on the Otto principle. Their NOx and methane-slip behaviour, the MARPOL Annex VI NOx Tiers and NOx Emission Control Areas, the IGF and IGC Codes, and the newest exhaust-energy machines — power turbine generator, hybrid and electric-assist turbochargers — complete the picture.
why: Simon's favourite machinery question is still 'ME versus MC'. The basic table is in Simon Notes; the marks now come from the depth — HPS, HCU, FIVA, CCU, redundancy — and from not calling ME a common-rail engine.

Dual-fuel engines are on the order books, and the two LNG concepts behave oppositely. ME-GI: high pressure, no knock, very low slip, Tier II without after-treatment. ME-GA: low pressure, knock-sensitive, more slip, Tier III with its standard EGR — except in SDF mode.

The Tier III question is now an ECA-by-ECA question. The Canadian Arctic and Norwegian Sea ECAs entered into force on 1 March 2026 and the North-East Atlantic ECA has been adopted; one '2016' date is no longer an answer.
Methane slip is now priced. Methane counts under the EU ETS from 1 January 2026 and under FuelEU Maritime, so the Chief Engineer's running mode and load profile on a gas engine have a direct cost.

sections.head: 🖥️ The ME Platform — What 'Electronically Controlled' Really Means

body.p: The MC-versus-ME comparison table — what the ME eliminates (camshaft, chain drive, fuel cams, roller guides, starting-air distributor, mechanical governor) and what replaces it — is already taught in Simon Notes Part 5 · Note 7. This topic goes deeper: how the hydraulics, valves and controllers fit together, and how the system behaves when part of it fails.

Not a common-rail engine. The source says the ME has 'no individual fuel pump for each unit but uses a common rail system'. That is wrong for the ME. Each cylinder has its own electronically controlled, hydraulically driven fuel-oil pressure booster on its HCU. What is common is the hydraulic oil supply at about 300 bar from the HPS; fuel reaches the boosters at low supply pressure. A fuel common rail — fuel stored at injection pressure and distributed to the injectors — is the WinGD RT-flex/X principle.

ME-C and ME-B. The large-bore ME-C (and the ME-GI, ME-GA and ME-LGI built on it) has no camshaft and no camshaft chain drive. The small-bore ME-B keeps a light camshaft, chain-driven, for the exhaust valves and controls only fuel injection electronically.

The ECU, ACU, EICU, SCU and CWCU run on identical MPC hardware with different software; on current ME and ME-C engines the CCU runs on a downsized controller, the MPC10. The MPC fitted at each cylinder is the CCU because it runs the CCU software.

body.p: The command chain. The tacho system gives the ECU the crank position; the ECU sends timing commands to the CCU; the CCU drives the actuator (the source's 'proportional coil') of a proportional multi-way valve; the valve admits ~300 bar hydraulic oil under the booster's hydraulic piston; the piston drives the fuel plunger and fuel is injected. The CCU positions the valve by an electrical command signal with position feedback.

The valve's opening (signal level) and opening duration set the booster plunger's stroke and speed, so the injected quantity follows the strength and duration of the command, not a fixed cam stroke and helix. Injection pressure is the hydraulic pressure multiplied by the booster's area ratio. The booster has a suction valve and no helix or spill port.

sections.head: 🛡️ Redundancy and Failure Behaviour — Going Deeper than the MC/ME Table

body.p: Everllence's ME Engine Control System is designed so that no single failure related to the system may cause the engine to stop. In most cases a single failure does not affect performance or power availability, or does so only partly by activating a slow-down (project guide 16.01, 'Units, layout and interfaces'):

ul: ECU — two in parallel; if one fails the other takes over without interruption.
CCU — all identical; a CCU failure automatically cuts out only that cylinder.
ACU — auxiliary control divided among three units so that one failure leaves enough redundancy for continued operation; HPS pump control is split between them.
HPS — multiple engine-driven and electric pumps with stand-by; high-pressure pipes to the HCUs are double-walled, and emergency running is possible using the outer pipe as pressure containment.
Networks and panels — redundant control networks A and B; two MOPs; tacho sets A and B.
Repair on the run — any controller can be replaced without stopping the engine, which returns to normal operation once the defective unit is replaced.

body.p: The oil is a control fluid. On the ME engine the system oil is also the hydraulic medium for the HPS and HCUs, so cleanliness and water content in the system oil matter to the control valves as well as to the bearings — the oil-analysis link in Topic 1.

sections.head: 🔥 Why Gas and Alternative-Fuel Engines — and the ME Family

body.p: The source gives three reasons: efficiency, NOx and the IMO GHG Strategy. Corrected: two-stroke dual-fuel engines have thermal efficiency comparable to diesel operation, so efficiency is not the main driver. The real drivers are lower SOx and particulates and lower CO2 per kWh when burning methane (partly offset by methane slip), fuel cost and availability, and — on gas carriers — the use of cargo boil-off gas. On NOx, only the low-pressure Otto-cycle engine is Tier III in gas mode without after-treatment; the high-pressure Diesel-cycle engine is Tier II. On GHG, the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy is resolution MEPC.377(80) — not part of Annex VI. Its in-force short-term measures are EEXI, CII and SEEMP; the fuel-intensity rules of the Net-Zero Framework remain draft and not adopted (Part 22 · Topic 3). Methane, ethane and methanol all contain carbon; only ammonia (and hydrogen) are carbon-free at the funnel.

body.p: Product status (as of 8 October 2026). Trade-press reports citing MAN Energy Solutions customer communication stated that ME-GA was withdrawn from new sales on 18 October 2024; existing installed engines remain relevant and supported. The ME-GA therefore matters to the Chief Engineer as an installed-fleet engine on LNG carriers, not as a new-build choice: Everllence's LNG dual-fuel two-stroke offering continues on the ME-GI. The ME-GA data in this topic (gas admission, EGR, operating modes) describe that installed design as set out in the Everllence project guide.

Knock versus pre-ignition. The source attributes ME-GA knock to 'pre-ignition'. They are different abnormal-combustion events. Knock is auto-ignition of the unburnt end-gas after the pilot has ignited the charge; pre-ignition is ignition before the pilot — from hot spots or lube-oil droplets. A premixed Otto engine is exposed to both; a Diesel-principle engine has no premixed charge and neither problem.

Operating modes on the ME-GA. Dual-fuel (gas) mode is started manually by the operator on the MOP. Specified dual-fuel (SDF) mode — activated only by the fuel-gas supply system — burns a mixture of gas and fuel oil within a gas flow limit, at reduced efficiency, increased methane slip and increased NOx; it is not IMO certified, and when it is logged an alarm is released and the bridge receives an indication of lack of Tier III compliance. The control and safety system fails to safe: any failure detected during gas running stops the gas, changes over to fuel oil and the gas system is purged with inert gas.

sections.head: 🌡️ How NOx Forms — Temperature, Residence Time, Oxygen

body.p: Atmospheric nitrogen is normally inert, but at very high temperature it combines with oxygen — the thermal (Zeldovich) NOx mechanism. Engine-out NOx is mostly NO, oxidising to NO2 later; the limits are expressed as NO2. Fuel-bound nitrogen adds a minor 'fuel NOx' share with residual fuels. Three factors govern thermal NOx:

'High temp inside chamber (1100 °C)' — not the NOx-forming temperature
How long the burned gas stays above that temperature
'How long the temp is maintained' — correct

body.p: Why the ME-GI stays at Tier II. In the ME-GI the gas is injected at high pressure into hot compressed air after the pilot oil has ignited, and it burns as it enters — a diffusion flame, exactly as with fuel oil. The flame zones burn close to stoichiometric, so local temperatures are very high and oxygen surrounds them: ideal conditions for thermal NOx. Engine-out NOx is therefore at Tier II level in both gas and fuel-oil modes, and Tier III needs EGR (less oxygen, more heat capacity in the charge) or SCR. Combustion lasts only tens of crank-angle degrees — milliseconds — so 'a very long time at high temperature' is the wrong picture.

Why the ME-GA is low-NOx in gas mode. The ME-GA burns a lean, premixed gas-air charge. Because the excess air is spread evenly through the charge, there are no hot near-stoichiometric flame zones and the peak flame temperature stays well below that of diffusion combustion. With a lower peak temperature, little time is spent above the temperature at which NOx forms quickly. Premixed flame propagation is not 'gradual' — the difference is temperature, not speed. The NOx countermeasures in general (EGR, SCR, Miller timing, HAM) are taught in Part 4 · Topic 19.

sections.head: 💨 Methane Slip

body.p: Definition. Methane slip is methane that is not burnt in the combustion chamber and leaves with the exhaust gas. It is highest in low-pressure Otto-cycle engines, where gas is mixed with air before ignition: premixed charge trapped in crevice volumes — the piston top land and ring pack — is not reached by the flame; in four-stroke engines gas can also short-circuit to the exhaust during valve overlap; and combustion is less complete at low load. A high-pressure Diesel-cycle engine has no gas in the cylinder during compression and scavenging, so its slip is very low.

Why it matters. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. IMO's 2024 LCA Guidelines (MEPC.391(81), non-mandatory) count methane with a 100-year global warming potential of 28 (IPCC AR5). Under EU law, FuelEU Maritime (from 1 January 2025) counts methane slip on a well-to-wake basis using default slip factors by engine type, unless verified actual values are used, and the EU ETS covers methane from 1 January 2026. The IMO LCA default factors by engine class are tabulated in Part 25 · Topic 1, and methane's place among the greenhouse gases in Part 22 · Topic 2; the IMO Net-Zero Framework remains a draft, not adopted (Part 22 · Topic 3).

qa: Q1. Is the ME engine a common-rail engine? Describe its fuel-injection system.

No. In the MAN B&W, now Everllence, ME engine each cylinder has its own fuel-oil pressure booster on its Hydraulic Cylinder Unit. The common element is the hydraulic oil supply at about 300 bar from the Hydraulic Power Supply, which is engine-driven as standard, with electric start-up pumps, and is a separate unit from the HCUs. Fuel is supplied to the boosters at low pressure. The Engine Control Unit, using crank position from the duplicated tacho system, sends timing commands to the Cylinder Control Unit, which positions a proportional valve — ELFI for fuel and ELVA for the exhaust valve, or a single FIVA for both. The valve admits hydraulic oil under the booster piston and the plunger injects fuel. Injection pressure is the hydraulic pressure times the booster area ratio, and quantity and rate follow the valve command, because there is no helix or spill port. A true fuel common rail, with fuel stored at injection pressure, is the WinGD RT-flex and X design.
Q2. What happens on an ME engine if one control unit fails?

The Engine Control System is designed so that no single failure related to the system may cause the engine to stop. There are two ECUs in parallel, one in hot stand-by, which takes over without interruption. There is one CCU per cylinder, all identical; if one fails, only that cylinder is cut out. Auxiliary control is divided among three ACUs, which also share control of the HPS pumps, so one failure leaves enough redundancy. The HPS has stand-by pumps, and the high-pressure pipes to the HCUs are double-walled so that emergency running is possible using the outer pipe. Control networks A and B, two MOPs and tacho sets A and B are duplicated. Any controller can be replaced without stopping the engine. In most cases a single failure has no effect on power, or only causes a slow-down.
Q3. Compare the ME-GI and ME-GA dual-fuel engines.

The ME-GI works on the Diesel principle: pilot oil is injected first and ignites, and gas is then injected at high pressure, up to 300 bar at the engine inlet, and burns as it enters. There is no premixed charge, so there is no knock and methane slip is very low, but engine-out NOx is at Tier II in both modes and Tier III needs EGR or SCR. The ME-GA works on the Otto principle in gas mode: gas is admitted at low pressure, which Everllence gives as 5.5 to 12 barg at the engine inlet depending on load and rating, through safe gas admission valves in the cylinder liner during the compression stroke. The lean premixed charge is ignited by about 0.5% pilot oil from a micro booster valve. That gives low NOx, but the engine is susceptible to knock and pre-ignition and has higher methane slip. Its design specifies EGR as standard (Everllence project guide), which ensures Tier III in dual-fuel and fuel-oil-only modes and cuts slip by up to half, but Tier III is not guaranteed in specified dual-fuel mode. The ME-GA's low-pressure gas plant is cheaper; the ME-GI needs a high-pressure compressor or pump.
Q4. State the NOx Tier limits and explain where Tier III applies.

Under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 13, for engines over 130 kW, with n the rated speed: Tier I is 17.0 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 45 times n to the power minus 0.2 from 130 to below 2000 rpm, and 9.8 at 2000 rpm and above, for ships constructed from 1 January 2000 to before 1 January 2011. Tier II is 14.4, 44 times n to the minus 0.23, and 7.7, for ships constructed on or after 1 January 2011. Tier III is 3.4, 9 times n to the minus 0.2, and 2.0 — about 80% below Tier I. Tier III applies only inside a NOx Emission Control Area, and each ECA has its own construction date: 1 January 2016 for the North American and US Caribbean ECAs; 1 January 2021 for the Baltic and North Sea; 1 January 2025 for the Canadian Arctic; and 1 March 2026 for the Norwegian Sea, by building contract, keel or delivery date. Both entered into force on 1 March 2026. The North-East Atlantic ECA was adopted in May 2026 and enters into force on 1 September 2027. The Mediterranean ECA is for sulphur and particulates only. Outside ECAs, a Tier III ship meets Tier II.
Q5. How is NOx formed in a diesel engine, and why is the ME-GI not Tier III without after-treatment?

NOx is mainly thermal NOx: nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine at very high temperature. Its formation depends on peak local temperature — it becomes significant above roughly 1,800 to 2,000 kelvin in the flame zones — on the residence time at that temperature, and on oxygen availability. More fuel raises NOx only indirectly, by raising temperature. In the ME-GI, gas is injected into hot air after the pilot ignites and burns as a diffusion flame. The flame zones are near stoichiometric and very hot, with oxygen around them, just as with fuel oil, so engine-out NOx is at Tier II. To reach Tier III it needs EGR, which lowers the oxygen and raises the heat capacity of the charge, or SCR, which removes NOx from the exhaust. The ME-GA in gas mode burns a lean premixed charge with no hot stoichiometric zones, so its peak temperature, and its NOx, are much lower.
Q6. Distinguish a power turbine generator, a hybrid turbocharger and an electric-assist turbocharger.

A power turbine generator is not a turbocharger. It is a separate exhaust-gas turbine in a bypass of the main-engine exhaust that drives a generator through a gearbox — turbo-compounding. It recovers surplus exhaust energy as electricity when the turbochargers are efficient enough to spare some exhaust flow, and it is shut down at low load. A hybrid turbocharger, such as Mitsubishi's MET-MAG, has a high-speed generator/motor coupled to the turbocharger rotor. It generates electricity from surplus exhaust energy, and in motoring mode it drives the rotor at low load in place of the auxiliary blowers. An electric-assist turbocharger has a motor on the compressor shaft that supplies energy to accelerate the rotor at low load for better scavenging. The first two take energy out of the exhaust; electric assist puts energy into the rotor.

deep_dive.title: Case Study — Entering a NOx ECA on an ME-GA LNG Carrier
blocks: An LNG carrier with Everllence B&W ME-GA main engines, built for Tier III ECA trading, is bound for a North Sea terminal. Boil-off is low after a long ballast leg, and the fuel-gas supply system has the engines running in specified dual-fuel (SDF) mode, burning a gas–fuel-oil mixture within its gas-flow limit. The bridge reports an indication of 'lack of Tier III compliance' 24 hours before the ECA boundary.
What the Chief Engineer works through

Why the alarm. Everllence states that SDF mode is a compromise — reduced efficiency, increased methane slip and increased NOx — that it is not IMO certified and that Tier III is not guaranteed in it; when SDF is logged the system raises an alarm and gives the bridge this indication. Compliant options inside the ECA. The engine's standard EGR ensures Tier III in dual-fuel (gas) mode with minimum pilot oil and in fuel-oil-only mode. So before the boundary the engines must be in one of those two modes: gas mode if enough boil-off or forced vaporisation can sustain the required load, otherwise fuel-oil-only with EGR. Evidence. The changeover time, position and mode are recorded as the Tier and on/off status record and in the Record Book of Engine Parameters; the EGR system's readiness — water treatment and bleed-off — is checked in advance. Methane. Leaving SDF also cuts methane slip, which now carries a cost under the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime.

'Tier III engine' describes what the engine can do in its certified modes, not what it does in every mode. The Chief Engineer plans the ECA entry like a fuel changeover — mode, time, position and record — and the oral answer should say exactly that.

(2) Top bracing (P29-C147): it does not 'transmit the vibration to the hull'. It stiffens the engine–double-bottom system so that the natural frequency rises above the running speed range — it is a detuner (P29-C149). (3) Viscous damper action (P29-C143): the relative motion is circumferential, not radial — the casing twists with the crankshaft while the inertia ring rotates steadily, shearing the silicone film. topics.definition: A two-stroke crosshead engine excites the ship in four ways (MAN B&W): external unbalanced moments from the inertia of the moving masses (first order, vertical and horizontal; second order, vertical only); guide-force moments, the lateral moments from the crosshead guide forces that rock (H-type) or twist (X-type) the engine top; axial vibration of the crankshaft, excited by gas forces deflecting the crank throws and passed to the hull through the thrust bearing; and torsional vibration of the shaft system, excited by the varying torque from gas pressure and the crank mechanism. Each becomes a problem at resonance, when the engine speed multiplied by the order of excitation equals a natural frequency of the engine, shaft line or hull. The countermeasures are an axial vibration damper, torsional design (shaft diameter, tuning wheel, dampers, barred speed range), lateral top bracing and moment compensators.
why: Simon sorts the four excitations quickly. A candidate who calls guide-force vibration 'longitudinal', or says top bracing 'passes vibration to the hull', has shown he does not know the mechanism.
The barred speed range is the Chief Engineer's daily limit. It comes from torsional resonance and class stress limits, and the engine must pass through it quickly — not run in it (Part 24 · Topic 2).

Vibration complaints arrive after delivery. Heavy vibration in the accommodation in ballast or at one speed is often a hull resonance with an engine moment; the remedy — compensator, top bracing or a damper — depends on the order and the node position.

The hardware needs looking after. Axial and torsional dampers, top-bracing units and compensator drives are machinery items on the planned maintenance system, and a failed damper can turn a harmless critical into a cracked crankshaft.

OEM paper and source of this block's figures: four excitation categories, compensators, top bracing, axial damper, torsional design and barred speed ranges, with service cases.
Classification society rules — torsional vibration

Class requires the torsional vibration characteristics of the engine–shafting system to be calculated and sets limits for the additional stress: a lower limit that may be exceeded only briefly (hence a barred speed range) and an upper limit that may not be exceeded at all. Shaft diameter is set by class rules; a reduced diameter needs higher-strength material.
ISO recommendations — ship vibration levels
Measured hull and accommodation vibration is judged against ISO recommended levels; compensators are fitted only where those would be exceeded (MAN).
ABS — Insights into Ship Vibration Analysis (June 2022)
Hull girder modes described by their number of nodes; engine-excited resonance with hull modes.

sections.head: 📐 Vibration Basics — Excitation, Order, Natural Frequency and Nodes

body.p: Every elastic system — crankshaft, shaft line, engine frame, hull girder — has natural frequencies, each with its own mode shape. A hull girder mode is named by its nodes, the points that do not move: the source's sketch shows a 2-node and a 3-node vertical mode. An engine produces forces and moments at whole multiples of its rotational speed — the orders. Resonance, and large vibration, occur where engine speed × order = a natural frequency; the deflection then depends on the excitation, the damping, and how close the frequencies are. A compensating force placed at or near a node has no effect, because it produces no moment about that node.

1st order: vertical and horizontal. 2nd order: vertical
